title: “WHOM SHALL I SEND?” — THE TERRIFYING PART OF ISAIAH 6 WE RARELY PREACH AFTER “SEND ME”
paragraphs: “WHOM SHALL I SEND?” — THE TERRIFYING PART OF ISAIAH 6 WE RARELY PREACH AFTER “SEND ME”
Everybody loves Isaiah’s “Here am I; send me.” Far fewer people keep reading long enough to discover where God was sending him—and what obedience was going to cost.
There is a version of Isaiah 6 that fits beautifully on a coffee mug.
“Here am I. Send me!”
It sounds courageous.
It sounds adventurous.
It sounds like the beginning of something extraordinary.
And it is.
But there is something almost unsettling about the way we sometimes quote those words.
Because we stop reading.
We celebrate the surrender without reading the assignment.
We preach the availability of Isaiah, but sometimes quietly walk away before hearing what God actually told the available man to do.
And if you have ever told Jesus, “Use me,” while secretly imagining what being used by Him would look like…
Isaiah 6 may disturb you.
Because sometimes God answers, “Send me,” by sending you somewhere you never would have chosen, to people who may not applaud, carrying truth they may not want to hear.
The story begins not with Isaiah volunteering.
It begins with a death.
“In the year that king Uzziah died…”
Isaiah 6:1.
A king was gone.
A throne on earth had become empty.
But Isaiah looked higher and discovered that the ultimate throne had never been vacant.
“I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up…”
That changes everything.
Before Isaiah becomes a messenger, Isaiah becomes a witness.
Before he sees the mission, he sees the Majesty.
Before he says, “Send me,” he encounters the holiness of the One doing the sending.
Seraphim cry to one another:
“Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.”
The Hebrew is breathtaking:
קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ
Qādôš, qādôš, qādôš.
Holy.
Holy.
Holy.
Not “Isaiah, Isaiah, Isaiah.”
Not “calling, calling, calling.”
Not “success, influence, platform.”
Holy.
The center of Isaiah 6 is not the greatness of a willing prophet.
It is the holiness of an incomparable God.
The foundations shake.
The house fills with smoke.
And suddenly Isaiah does something that should make every person who wants to be “used by God” think carefully.
He does not introduce himself.
He does not announce his qualifications.
He does not tell God about his potential.
He falls apart.
“Woe is me! for I am undone…”
The Hebrew begins:
אוֹי־לִי
’Ôy-lî.
“Woe to me.”
Then comes the devastating confession:
כִּי אִישׁ טְמֵא־שְׂפָתַיִם אָנֹכִי
Ki ’ish teme-sefatayim anokhi.
In sense: “For I am a man of unclean lips.”
Isaiah had been speaking prophetic woes over others.
Then he saw God.
And suddenly the sinner he could see most clearly was himself.
That is what genuine encounters with holiness do.
They do not merely make us emotional about everybody else’s sin.
They expose ours.
Maybe that is where this story has to become personal.
It is easy to look at a collapsing culture and say, “Woe to them.”
Easy to point at the addict.
The adulterer.
The hypocrite.
The corrupt leader.
The compromised church.
The rebellious generation.
The person whose sins happen to be more visible than yours.
But then the throne comes into view.
And suddenly you remember the messages you deleted.
The bitterness you renamed “discernment.”
The lust you kept feeding.
The apology you never gave.
The forgiveness you keep withholding.
The secret habit nobody at church knows about.
The pride hidden underneath your theology.
The prayer life that has quietly become almost nonexistent.
The private version of you that would terrify the public version of you if it ever became visible.
And before a holy God, Isaiah does not say, “At least I am better than them.”
He says, essentially:
I am unclean too.
But this is where Isaiah 6 becomes Gospel-shaped long before Bethlehem.
God does not leave the confessed sinner standing there condemned.
A seraph takes a burning coal from the altar.
It touches Isaiah’s lips.
And Isaiah hears words every guilty soul longs to hear:
“Thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged.”
Do not rush past that.
Isaiah did not cleanse himself before volunteering.
Grace touched him first.
The altar came before the assignment.
Cleansing came before commissioning.
Forgiveness came before sending.
That pattern matters because Christianity is not the story of sinful people making themselves impressive enough for God to employ.
It is the story of grace reaching the unclean.
And what Isaiah experiences symbolically around the altar points us toward something infinitely greater revealed fully in Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, our hope is not a coal touching our lips.
Our hope is the crucified and risen Son of God bearing sin and accomplishing redemption.
Peter writes that Christ “bare our sins in his own body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
Paul says that in Christ “we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins” (Ephesians 1:7).
Isaiah needed cleansing.
So do you.
So do I.
And the Gospel declares that forgiveness is not found in pretending we were never dirty.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
Then—and only then—comes the question.
Isaiah hears the voice of the Lord:
אֶת־מִי אֶשְׁלַח וּמִי יֵלֶךְ־לָנוּ
’Et-mi ’eshlach, umi yelekh-lanu?
“Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?”
And Isaiah answers:
הִנְנִי שְׁלָחֵנִי
Hineni, shelacheni.
“Here am I; send me.”
Hineni.
Here I am.
Not merely, “I am standing at this geographical location.”
It is availability.
Presence.
Readiness.
Here I am.
And perhaps you have prayed something like it.
“Jesus, use me.”
“Lord, send me.”
“God, whatever You want.”
Beautiful words.
Dangerous words.
Because God answers Isaiah.
And this is where the coffee-mug version usually ends.
The Bible does not.
God tells him:
“Go.”
But what follows is not a promise that thousands will immediately repent.

Isaiah receives a severe prophetic commission to a spiritually resistant people. He is to proclaim God's word in the midst of hardened hearing and blinded perception, and Isaiah eventually asks the agonizing question:
“Lord, how long?”
Think about that.
Isaiah said, “Send me.”
God did.
And the assignment included rejection.
The man who saw the throne would now speak to people who often would not listen.
The man whose lips had been cleansed would use those lips to proclaim truth that would expose hardened hearts.
His obedience could not be measured merely by applause.
His faithfulness could not be measured merely by visible results.
And suddenly Isaiah 6 becomes painfully relevant.
Because maybe you thought obedience would make everybody understand you.
Maybe you thought following Jesus would automatically repair every relationship.
Maybe you thought sharing biblical truth would guarantee appreciation.
Maybe you thought serving faithfully meant your ministry would explode.
Maybe you thought raising your children in Christ guaranteed they would never wander.
Maybe you thought praying faithfully meant the answer would arrive quickly.
Maybe you thought, “Send me,” meant God would send you somewhere glamorous.
Instead He sent you back into that difficult home.
Into that workplace.
Into that marriage that needs patient faithfulness.
Into conversations nobody applauds.
Into years of praying for someone who still seems far from God.
Into serving when almost nobody notices.
Into telling the truth lovingly when silence would have been easier.
And somewhere inside you a question begins forming.
“Lord… how long?”
How long do I keep praying?
How long do I keep forgiving?
How long do I keep serving?
How long do I keep sharing Christ with someone who keeps rejecting Him?
How long do I remain faithful when faithfulness feels invisible?
Isaiah asked that question too.
And this is one of the truths we desperately need to recover:
Your assignment is obedience.
The results belong to God.
That does not mean results do not matter. Scripture repeatedly cares about fruit.
It means visible success is not the sovereign judge of faithfulness.
Noah preached righteousness in a wicked generation.
Jeremiah spoke while people resisted him.
The apostles suffered for proclaiming Christ.
And Jesus Himself was abandoned by many who had once followed Him.
So perhaps the question is not merely:
“Will God use me?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“Will I still obey Him when being used by Him looks nothing like what I imagined?”
Will you still say hineni when nobody claps?
Will you still say shelacheni when obedience costs something?
Will you still speak truth with love when truth becomes unpopular?
Will you still follow Christ when Christianity stops being convenient?
Will you still serve when your name is forgotten?
Will you still forgive when your flesh wants revenge?
Will you still pray when heaven seems silent?
Will you still carry the Gospel when the people you love roll their eyes?
That is where “Here am I” becomes more than Christian merchandise.
It becomes surrender.
But there is another astonishing detail.
Isaiah's story does not ultimately terminate in judgment.
The book bearing his name keeps moving.
Through warnings.
Through tears.
Through judgment.
Through promises.
Until the horizon begins glowing with Someone Isaiah could not yet see in Bethlehem but whom God was already revealing through prophecy.
A child would be born.
A Son would be given.
A Servant would suffer.
A wounded Savior would bear the sins of others.
“He was wounded for our transgressions…”
Isaiah 53:5.
Centuries later, Jesus Christ came.

And when the Gospel of John reflects on Isaiah's vision, it makes an astonishing Christ-centered connection: after quoting from Isaiah 6, John says Isaiah “saw his glory, and spake of him” (John 12:41).
The throne of Isaiah 6 and the cross of the Gospel are not competing pictures.
The Holy One we cannot domesticate is the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
The God before whom Isaiah cried “Woe is me” is not indifferent to ruined people.
In Christ, He came for them.
That includes you.
Your scandal is not stronger than His grace.
Your history is not stronger than His blood.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
Your secret sin should be confessed, not protected.
Your guilt should drive you toward Christ, not deeper into hiding.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the mercy of God calling you out of the grave you were decorating.
Jesus does not merely make bad people appear respectable.
He makes spiritually dead people alive.
So maybe your first response today should not be:
“Send me.”
Maybe it should be:
“Woe is me.”
Maybe before asking God for a platform, you need the altar.
Before asking Him to enlarge your influence, you need Him to expose your heart.
Before saying, “Use my mouth,” perhaps you need to surrender what your mouth has been saying.
Before asking for a calling, perhaps you need repentance.
Because God is not looking for actors who know how to appear holy.
He calls sinners.
Cleanses sinners.
Transforms sinners.
And then sends forgiven sinners to tell other sinners where mercy can be found.
That is why your past does not automatically disqualify you from becoming a testimony of grace.
Peter denied Jesus and was restored.
Paul had persecuted the church and became a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The woman of Samaria carried the news of Jesus back toward people who knew her complicated story.
Again and again, Scripture reveals a God whose grace does not pretend the scandal never happened.
Grace does something better.
It redeems.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by pretending sin does not matter.
Not by lowering God's holiness until nobody needs repentance.
Jesus rewrites everything by confronting sin, bearing judgment, offering forgiveness, raising the dead, restoring the broken, and creating new lives that could never have written themselves.
So here is the question Isaiah 6 leaves burning in the room:
If Jesus has forgiven you…
where is He sending you?
Maybe it is not across an ocean.
Maybe it is across the hallway.
Maybe your mission field has your last name.
Maybe it sits beside you at work.
Maybe it is the friend whose jokes hide depression.
Maybe it is the child who stopped going to church.
Maybe it is the spouse you stopped praying for because disappointment became easier than hope.
Yes.
Even there.
What if the article you share becomes the article somebody reads alone at 2:13 in the morning while trying desperately not to collapse?
You cannot save them.
Gospel Warrior cannot save them.
A preacher cannot save them.
Only Jesus saves.
But someone can carry the message.
“Whom shall I send?”
Perhaps tagging that friend is not about engagement at all.
Perhaps it is you saying, “I thought of you, and I refuse to let embarrassment keep me silent.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you have been exhausted but you refuse to abandon your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to remember you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”
And if God is confronting you about something you already know He has been asking you to surrender, comment, “Here am I.”
Not for performance.
Not to impress strangers.
As a small public confession that you do not want to keep running.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding you with Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical teaching, and reminders that continually lead you back to Jesus, you can also help this work continue.
It does not.
It does not.
And not because anyone should be pressured into giving. Scripture says plainly that giving must not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 9:7).

But Scripture also gives us a beautiful picture of believers voluntarily partnering in Gospel work. The Philippians repeatedly supported Paul's ministry, and Paul described their generosity as “an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God” (Philippians 4:16–18).
That is the spirit in which we invite you.

Your support helps us keep creating and distributing Christ-centered content, biblical encouragement, discipleship materials, and resources designed to reach the wounded, the wandering, the curious, the struggling believer, and the person who may be one Gospel encounter away from finally crying out to Jesus.
Send it privately to the person God just brought to your mind.
Because the mission was never supposed to stop with the person who received the message.
Someone carried the Gospel until it reached you.
Now somebody else may be waiting for someone willing to carry it to them.
And perhaps that is the part of Isaiah 6 we have avoided.
“Send me” was never merely a beautiful sentence.
It was permission.
Permission for God to interrupt Isaiah's plans.
Permission to speak through cleansed lips.
Permission to send him toward difficult people.
Permission to remain faithful when visible results were painful.
Permission to keep going long enough to ask:
“Lord, how long?”
Maybe you are standing there now.
Tired.
Disappointed.
Still carrying scars from your own scandal.
Still wondering whether God could possibly use someone with your history.
Look again.
The story did not begin with Isaiah's usefulness.
It began with God's holiness.
Isaiah confessed.
God cleansed.
God called.
Isaiah answered.
And that same Gospel rhythm still destroys our excuses today.
See His holiness.
Confess your sin.
Run to Christ.
Receive the mercy purchased at the cross.
Rise in grace.
Then go wherever your King sends you.
Not because you are spotless.
Because Jesus saves sinners.
Not because you are fearless.
Because Christ is worthy.
Not because everyone will listen.
Because the One who sends you deserves your yes.
So when heaven asks…
“Whom shall I send?”
May your answer no longer be a verse you merely admire.
May it become the surrender by which you live.
And when your voice trembles as you say “Here am I,” remember: the God who sends you already knows every chapter behind you—and through Jesus Christ, grace can still write what comes next.
